title: StringBuilder.append is quadratic in jolt, so JSON on long strings crawls
description:
MISDIAGNOSED WHEN FILED, corrected 2026-08-12. The original text blamed clojure.data.json and cited ~700 bytes/sec (2KB=2.9s, 8KB=10.6s, 32KB=44.7s). Those numbers do not reproduce and were measured over nREPL while gen-18 had a beam of 4 plus the Lean pool saturating the box; they are contention, not the parser.

Measured on an idle machine, data.json parses at 0.0003-0.0004 ms/char (~2.5 MB/s) when the payload is many short values, and stays flat. It degrades only as a SINGLE string value grows: 0.0025 ms/char at 2KB rising to 0.0068 at 64KB. That is superlinear in one value, not slow overall.

ROOT CAUSE, in jolt and not in veriframe: host/chez/java/host-static-classes.ss defined

  (cons "append" (lambda (self x . rest) (sb-set! self (string-append (sb-str self) (append-text x rest))) self))

Every append copied the whole accumulated buffer, so building an n-char string was O(n^2). StringWriter.write and PrintWriter's write-through to either had the same shape. data.json reads a quoted string one character at a time into a StringBuilder, which is why a long string value was the only shape that hurt.

Veriframe hits it in both directions. The largest real witness (88103 chars, a flat map whose countA value is one ~87KB SMT-LIB string) took 623ms to read and 672ms to write.

FIXED in jolt a1856fbe: appends cons onto a pending chunk list, joined only when something reads the buffer; length/isEmpty/count answer from a running total so they do not force the join. Verified by test/chez/string-builder-perf.ss (make sbperf), which asserts a scaling ratio rather than a wall-clock floor: 16.1x for 4x the appends before, 3.2x after. jolt unit clean, corpus 4323/4332 with 0 new divergence, cts 6078 pass matching baseline, printperf within guards.

Result for that witness: read 623ms -> 200ms, write 672ms -> 89ms. Per-char cost is now flat at ~0.0022 instead of climbing.

REMAINING: veriframe runs the Homebrew jolt binary (0.7.5), which has the old host files baked in, so it does not see the fix until jolt is rebuilt and installed.
acceptance_criteria: A 32KB document parses in single-digit milliseconds, and the hot paths use the fast parser.
close_reason: Root-caused to jolt's quadratic StringBuilder/StringWriter append and fixed there (jolt fix/stringbuilder-quadratic-append, c22ce774). Verified: sbperf 16.1x -> 3.2x scaling, jolt unit clean, corpus 4323/4332 with 0 new divergence, cts 6078 matching baseline, veriframe suite 240 tests/1171 assertions clean under the fixed binary. Run-detail endpoint 322.7s -> 3.2s. No veriframe code change was needed for either.

title: The coverage rung blocks on words when only numbers were ever the point
description:
Run 0d0c3560, wind-down: B4 and B4.3 have between them made eleven done attempts and cannot ship. After three rounds of widening the stopword list the refusals are down to one or two words each, and they are still refusals: 'formed', 'banked', 'tested', 'legitimately', 'listing', 'individual', 'concrete'. Each round surfaces new ordinary English. It does not converge, and it has cost this run something like forty turns.

The rung's own docstring says what it is for: 'Numbers matter most — an answer naming a size, a bound, or a witness has to have that number in the evidence.' The number check is exact, cheap, and has never produced a false positive. The word check is a lexical proxy for 'does the answer assert something unsupported', a question the audit already answers with semantics and in context, and which it answered PASS for every one of these attempts.

Fix: numbers block, words advise. Uncovered numbers refuse done exactly as now. Uncovered words are journalled and handed to the AUDIT prompt, where a model can weigh in context whether they assert anything the evidence does not support — which is the gate that should have been asking all along.

This is not defence-in-depth removed; it is a proxy retired in favour of the check it was standing in for.
acceptance_criteria: A number in no artifact still refuses done. An audited answer is never refused over an English word, and the words the lexical check would have flagged reach the audit and the journal.
close_reason: Closed

title: The coverage rung forbids the exact vocabulary the relevance rung demands
description:
B4 of run 0d0c3560 called done eight times between t31 and t50 and burned about twenty turns on it. Its audit PASSED at t49. Six of the eight refusals came from the uncovered-tokens rung, listing as unsupported assertions: stated, facts, computation, checked, against, found, together, asked, settled, establish, evidence, showed, search, finding, proving, supported, general, partial, whenever, conditional, branch, selection, cardinality.

Almost none of those is an assertion. They are the words a model uses to FRAME one, which is what the stopword list already exists to exempt, and the list was last extended for exactly this ('does', 'from', 'having', 'follow').

Three separate causes, all mine:

1. CONTRADICTION WITH THE NEW RELEVANCE RUNG. That rung tells a branch to state which questions it did not settle and what it established instead. An honest partial answer must NAME the thing it failed to establish, and that thing is by construction absent from the evidence, so the coverage rung refuses the answer for containing it. The two rungs cannot both be satisfied. Introduced this morning.

2. NO MORPHOLOGICAL TOLERANCE. Matching is str/includes? against the raw haystack, so 'residues' misses 'residue', 'enumeration' misses 'enumerating', and 'optimal-flow' misses 'optimal flow'. Same stemming hole found in state/claim-tokens earlier today.

3. MISSING FRAMING VOCABULARY in the stopword list.

Fix, keeping the gate's actual purpose intact — numbers stay matched exactly against artifacts only, because fabricated numbers are what this rung is for. Word tokens get morphological and hyphen tolerance, and may also be covered by the passing audit's own ESTABLISHED restatement.
acceptance_criteria: A branch whose audit has passed can ship an honestly-scoped partial answer without the coverage rung refusing it for words like 'settled' or 'establish', and a number appearing in no artifact is still refused.
close_reason: Closed

title: A rejected artifact never told the branch what was wrong
description:
encoding-faithful? returned a bare boolean and discarded the reviewer's reasoning. Every engine then showed the branch generic boilerplate ('Check every coefficient, bound and index set against the claim's wording'), and the failure log — which IS cross-branch — recorded 'z3 returned unsat (status unfaithful)'.

Observed live on the phase-unwrap run, twice over:
- The reviewer found a sign error in one divergence equation and named the fix exactly: change (+ (- k4) (- k7)) to (+ k4 (- k7)). The branch got the boilerplate and resubmitted the IDENTICAL artifact the next turn.
- A vacuous-unsat objection ('proves uniqueness, never asserts the candidate is feasible') was learned by B1.2 at turn 18 and repeated verbatim by B1.2.3 at turn 27, because the cross-branch failure log carried only the boilerplate.

So the judge was doing high-quality work — three distinct defect classes caught, often with an exact fix — and none of it reached anyone.

Fixed: encoding-faithful? returns {:ok? :reason}, where reason is the structural warnings or the judge's text. All five call sites (prolog, smt, template, lean, octave) quote it to the branch, and the smt failure reason carries it into the cross-branch log.
acceptance_criteria: A rejection shows the branch the actual objection, and the failure log carries it.
close_reason: Fixed and hot-reloaded into the live run over nREPL. Test: a-rejection-quotes-the-objection-to-the-branch-and-the-failure-log.

title: Prolog verify has no faithfulness check and records only the goal name
description:
gen-13 (6f6704f4) artifact 333, branch B3.3.3 turn 21, is CONFIRMED and FALSE. Claim: 'The q=105 layered condition ... has a satisfying assignment' for the 45 3,5,7-smooth moduli <= 2000. It would be a major result — it implies the mod-15 condition is satisfiable at N=2000, since a mod-15 class's relative density is the average of its seven mod-105 sub-classes.

The rule (added turn 20 as q105_n2000) posts its class constraints inside findall/3:

  findall(., (between(0,104,C), class_terms(...), scalar_product(Coefs,Bs,#>=,L)), _),
  labeling([ff],Flat).

findall/3 runs its goal in a separate context and undoes bindings AND constraint posts on completion, so every density constraint is discarded before labeling runs. What remains is 'Row ins 0..1, sum(Row,#=,1)' — pick one residue per modulus — which is trivially satisfiable. Hence 10 instant solutions with empty witnesses.

Demonstrated in swipl:
  X in 0..1, findall(_, (X #>= 5), _), label([X])   -> succeeds, X=0
  X in 0..1, X #>= 5, label([X])                    -> fails

Two harness defects:

1. The vf-slr faithfulness judge is wired only into verify_smt. verify (prolog), verify_lean, verify_octave and verify_template have no equivalent, and this is the identical failure mode the judge exists to catch.

2. The prolog artifact's code column records only the goal ('sat_105'), not the rule body that defines it. The definition lives in an earlier add_rule turn, so the artifact is not self-contained and cannot be audited from the artifacts table alone. Whatever check gets added must see the rule text, and crossover/seeding must carry it.

Impact: the false claim is confirmed in a live run and reachable by other branches through the shared artifact log, where it argues the mod-105 direction is a dead end. The truth is the opposite — mod-15 is verified unsat through N=1500 and mod-105 is finer still.
acceptance_criteria: An engine-confirmed prolog artifact carries the rules its goal depends on, and a would-be confirmation is checked against its claim the way verify_smt is.
close_reason: Fixed in 965b459: prolog artifacts carry the assert log with the goal, would-be confirmations go through the same faithfulness judge as verify_smt (with a note naming findall/3, forall/2 and \+ as contexts that undo constraint posts), and the ground-goal path no longer reaches :confirmed on the strength of merely succeeding. Tests cover all three. NOT YET DEPLOYED to the running server — needs a restart to take effect.

title: Branch that forks twice reissues a child id and kills the run
description:
spawn-children! named children (str parent-id "." (+ batch-index 2)), with no memory of an earlier fork. A branch that forks a second time reissues .2, the INSERT fails 'UNIQUE constraint failed: branches.run_id, branches.id', the exception escapes run-rounds and the run dies.

Killed both campaign runs:
- gen-11 (90336412): B1.2 spawned B1.2.2/B1.2.3 at turn 25; repopulate invited it at 02:33:48; it called branch_theses at 02:34:26; next round collided. Silent, because start-run! swallowed the throw — this is the crash vf-92l was filed for and could not identify.
- gen-12 (98d0423e): B2.2 spawned B2.2.2/B2.2.3 at turn 24, forked again at turn ~43, same collision. Diagnosed in minutes because the vf-92l fix journaled the message and type.

Not a corner case. Repopulation asks the strongest survivor to branch again, and the strongest survivor is the one that has already branched, so any run that loses width twice hits it.

Fixed in beam/child-ids: allocate from the ids already in the branches table, skipping taken suffixes and filling gaps. Reads the DB rather than branch state so a resumed run is also correct.
acceptance_criteria: A parent can fork twice; ids stay unique; tests cover the allocator and a live double fork.
close_reason: Fixed in eda36a4: beam/child-ids allocates from the branches table, skipping taken suffixes. Tests cover the allocator and a live double fork. This was also the unidentified gen-11 crash from vf-92l.

title: Beam crash leaves run marked 'running' forever; exception swallowed to stdout
description:
Run 90336412 (gen-11) stopped at 02:34:46 with status still 'running' and ended_at NULL.

CORRECTED DIAGNOSIS (an earlier version of this issue blamed a Chez GC handshake; that was wrong — it profiled an unrelated process, /tmp/prog.clj, a core.async test spinning at 100%. Verified since: jolt honours deref timeouts on both futures and promises).

What actually happened: beam/run! threw. Evidence:
- harness (jolt serve, pid 62370) is IDLE — 10:37 CPU over 3h, no outbound sockets, no engine subprocesses
- ZERO swipl processes, though every live branch holds a prolog session -> run!'s finally ran and disposed them
- neither finish-run! call site (beam.clj:521 completed, :538 failed) was reached, since status is still 'running'

The swallow is api/control.clj start-run!:

  (catch Throwable e
    (log/error "run failed:" (ex-message e))
    {:status :error :error (ex-message e)})

It logs to the process's stdout (a tty) and returns a value nobody reads — the future's value is never dereferenced. The run row is never updated, (swap! active dissoc run-id) is skipped so abort! still thinks it is live, and nothing is journaled. The only record of the actual exception is a line in the user's terminal scrollback.

So a crash is indistinguishable from a healthy long-running round: same status, same absence of events. That is the real defect — not the underlying throw, which is still unidentified.
acceptance_criteria: A non-yielding branch turn forfeits within the deadline and the beam continues.
close_reason: Fixed in e0d30c3: run-rounds journals run-error and marks the row failed before rethrowing; start-run! drops the dead handle; runs/stalled? plus last_progress_at exposed on the run endpoint. Verified against the dead gen-11 run, which now reports stalled=true instead of claiming to be running.

title: Judge confirms SMT claims whose encoding doesn't match the claim text
description:
Gen-11 shipped three confirmed artifacts (P500 a#308, P600 a#313, P1000 a#311) asserting 'no subcollection satisfies the mod-3 layered necessary condition'. All three encode the WRONG condition: a modulus m divisible by 3 lands entirely inside one class mod 3, so its relative density in that class is 3/m, but all three encodings give it L/m (same coefficient as a coprime modulus) against a threshold of L. That understates 3-divisible contributions 3x, making the system strictly harder to satisfy, so unsat proves something weaker than the claim.

Verified with Z3 on a regenerated pool (identical moduli/lcm to the artifacts): as-encoded is unsat for N=300,315,500,600,1000; corrected (3L/m) is unsat for 300,315 and SAT for 500,600,1000. So the claims are false, not merely unsupported.

B1.3 diagnosed this itself and honourably abandoned rather than ship. The gate did not.

Root cause: nothing checks that the submitted encoding faithfully represents the claim text. The judge reads claim + verdict; the linter checks syntax. A mis-scaled coefficient is invisible to both.
acceptance_criteria: An encoding-faithfulness check exists that would reject these three artifacts; the three gen-11 artifacts are marked refuted/retracted in the journal.
notes: Follow-up coverage issue is vf-djx (not vf-2ky as written in the close reason).
close_reason: Fixed across 965b459 and a701e51. Coverage: verify_smt and verify (prolog) now run deterministic structural checks BEFORE the LLM judge, and the judge after. Validated against the real artifacts — a#333, a#338, a#343 rejected; a#337, a#345 accepted; no false positives. Remaining gaps tracked in vf-2ky: verify_lean, verify_octave and verify_template are still judge-free, and refutations skip both layers.

title: The GUI reported a failed start for a run that was starting fine
description:
Clicking start run in the UI showed an error while the same request succeeded over curl.

CAUSE. gui.api set :socket-timeout 10000 for every call. POST /v1/runs does not answer when the run row is written: api.control/start-run! blocks on (deref promised 30000), and beam/run! only calls on-start after opening every branch —

  run-id (runs/start-run! conn {...})        ; row committed, started_at set
  _ (when seed-run (artifacts/seed-from-run! ...))
  initial (mapv #(open-branch! ctx ...) (range width))
  (when on-start (on-start run-id))          ; response released here

so the server is allowed 30s and the client gave up at 10. Measured: 47ms on an idle machine, 21095ms moments later with the system busy. curl has no such limit, which is why the endpoint 'worked'.

Worse than a spurious error: the row is already committed and the beam keeps going, so the user was told the run failed AND left with a live run consuming provider spend. Reproduced exactly — GUI client returned 'Read timed out' while run 60381dbb was created and ran on.

FIXED. gui.api/start-timeout-ms is 40000, deliberately above the server's own 30s budget, and POST takes a per-call override (branch-detail already did this with 45s). Covered by gui_api_test — the assertion is that start-run!'s socket timeout exceeds 30000, so it cannot silently drift back under the server's window. Verified end to end against a live server: a start that took 21095ms now succeeds.

FOLLOW-UP worth considering separately: on-start fires after the whole beam is open, which is what makes this endpoint slow and variable. api.control/start-run! documents itself as returning 'immediately'. Moving on-start to just after the row insert would make it actually immediate, at the cost of handing out an id for a run whose branches do not exist yet.
close_reason: Fixed and verified end to end: start-timeout-ms 40000 outlasts the server's 30s window, gui_api_test asserts it stays above 30000, and a 21095ms start now succeeds where it previously returned 'Read timed out'.

title: veriframe runs the Homebrew jolt, which predates the StringBuilder fix
description:
The quadratic-append fix (vf-gff) lives in jolt's host/chez/java sources, which the standalone binary bakes in at build time. `which jolt` resolves to /opt/homebrew/bin/jolt -> ../Cellar/jolt/0.7.5/bin/jolt, so every normal veriframe invocation — jolt serve, jolt -M:test, jolt -M:gui — still runs the old quadratic code.

Measured under each, same DB, same 1154801-byte run-detail response: 322.7s on the Homebrew binary against 3.2s on the freshly built one.

Until jolt is rebuilt and installed, none of the win reaches a real run. Deciding HOW is an environment call, not something to do silently: 'make install' writes to $PREFIX/bin (~/.local/bin by default) which would shadow or diverge from the Homebrew-managed copy, and bumping the Homebrew formula is a separate release step. A build exists at ~/src/jolt-lang/jolt/target/release/jolt and can be used directly in the meantime.
acceptance_criteria: A jolt carrying c22ce774 is what `jolt` resolves to, and the run-detail endpoint measures in seconds rather than minutes through the HTTP server.
close_reason: jolt 0.7.6 is installed (Cellar/jolt/0.7.6, symlinked at /opt/homebrew/bin/jolt) and carries a1856fbe — the StringBuilder fix rode into main on PR #593. Verified against the installed binary: run-detail 322740ms -> 3344ms in-process and 3.33s through HTTP, 88KB witness read 352ms / write 255ms, veriframe suite 240 tests / 1171 assertions clean.

title: The run-detail endpoint was slow serializing its response, not parsing it
description:
The run-detail endpoint was slow, but NOT for the reason first filed. The original text blamed get-run parsing witnesses only to re-encode them and attributed 53s of a 64s endpoint to that round trip. Measured component by component against a live server on an idle box (2026-08-12), every data-gathering step is fast:

  get-run row      1 ms
  last-progress    2 ms
  stalled?         6 ms
  branches (15)   10 ms
  run-metrics    300 ms
  artifacts (122) 58 ms
  gate-tally       1 ms
  interventions    1 ms

That is ~380ms total. The cost is entirely in serializing the response: json/write-str over the assembled 1.15MB body. So the parse-then-re-encode framing was wrong; the write direction was the problem, and both were the same underlying defect — jolt's quadratic StringBuilder/StringWriter append (vf-gff).

This is why vf-8g2 was made to depend on vf-gff rather than fixed on its own: changing the response shape would have been a GUI-visible contract change that the root-cause fix made unnecessary.

AFTER vf-gff (jolt a1856fbe), same run, same machine, in-process:
  build-body  193 ms
  write-str  3052 ms
  total      3245 ms   (1154801 bytes)

against >300s before (curl timed out at 300s). No veriframe change was needed.

Residual, not yet chased: 1.15MB in 3.05s is ~380 KB/s, while the single 88KB witness now writes at ~1 MB/s. Nested structure costs more per node than one long string, so this may be ordinary per-node overhead rather than anything left over — but it has not been measured, and the endpoint is no longer pathological either way.
acceptance_criteria: /v1/runs/<id> returns in under a second on a run with 120+ artifacts, with the response shape either preserved or the GUI updated in the same change.
notes:
Exact A/B, same DB, same 1154801-byte response, in-process (no HTTP):

  old jolt    build-body 205 ms   write-str 322535 ms   total 322740 ms
  fixed jolt  build-body 193 ms   write-str   3052 ms   total   3245 ms

write-str 322.5s -> 3.05s, 106x. Data gathering was never the problem: it is ~200ms in both. 99.9% of the endpoint was serialization, which is vf-gff's quadratic StringBuilder in the write direction. No veriframe change made.
close_reason: Root-caused to jolt's quadratic StringBuilder/StringWriter append and fixed there (jolt fix/stringbuilder-quadratic-append, c22ce774). Verified: sbperf 16.1x -> 3.2x scaling, jolt unit clean, corpus 4323/4332 with 0 new divergence, cts 6078 matching baseline, veriframe suite 240 tests/1171 assertions clean under the fixed binary. Run-detail endpoint 322.7s -> 3.2s. No veriframe code change was needed for either.

title: The faithfulness judge failed proofs that prove more than the claim
description:
faithfulness-prompt told the judge to FAIL an artifact expressing something 'stronger, weaker, or simply different'. For the proving direction that is wrong: proving a universal by refuting its negation, an encoding that drops a hypothesis or leaves a sort unconstrained proves a harder theorem, and the claim follows from it.

gen-18 B4 T33 claimed a theorem about a finite set D and encoded D as an unconstrained SMT sort. Z3 returned unsat, proving it for every D. The judge failed it for formalising 'a stronger statement than the claimed finite-set theorem'. That was one of the three consecutive failures that culled B4 — the branch furthest along on Q-A, which had already closed two Lean proofs.

Polarity matters and inverts by direction: for a counterexample the witness must satisfy every hypothesis the claim makes, so generality is not licensed there.
acceptance_criteria: The proving prompt tells the judge a strictly more general formalisation is a PASS and explains that the claim follows from it, while still refusing extra hypotheses or narrowed domains. The refuting and measuring prompts are unchanged in this respect.
close_reason: Fixed, tested, deployed into run 65d50333 over nREPL.

title: An engine outage spent a branch's cull budget
description:
tools/fail set :category :failure on every path, including 'Lean is unavailable' / 'Octave is unavailable' / 'Mathlib search is unavailable'. Those are facts about the process pool, not about the branch.

gen-18 B3 was culled after six consecutive failures while pursuing the reduction of stage 2 to a separable convex cost flow — the strongest line in that run. One of the six was a Lean outage.
acceptance_criteria: An engine that cannot be reached returns a neutral turn and never raises consecutive-failures.
close_reason: Fixed, tested, deployed into run 65d50333 over nREPL.

title: A fork cannot cite a number its parent verified
description:
The done gate's coverage rung reads only (:artifacts branch). Artifacts confirmed elsewhere in the run reach a branch through the shared-artifact block in loop.clj (line 113-125) and the crossover block in beam.clj (line 60-64) — they enter the PROMPT and never the branch's artifact list. So the harness shows a branch evidence and then refuses the answer that cites it.

Concrete casualty this run (0d0c3560): B4.2.2.2 T92 was refused with 'Your answer states figures no artifact supports: 8, 6'. 8 and 6 are the m=3 optimal count and cost, exhaustively verified by Prolog CLPFD on its own parent B4.2.2 and shipped in B4.2.2's accepted answer at T73. The child rewrote its answer to drop them, and in the same edit also dropped its own Lean theorem flowopt_equiv_split (T82, confirmed, all m), so the accepted T94 answer says the explicit-graph link is 'verified at m=1' when the branch had proven it for every m.

This penalises exactly the structure the beam is built on. Every fork inherits its parent's reasoning and none of its evidence.
acceptance_criteria: A branch can cite a claim confirmed by any branch in the same run without the coverage rung refusing it, and the shipped answer attributes it. Regression test: two branches, one banks a numeric artifact, the other's answer states that number and passes.
close_reason: Done gate now reads run-wide confirmed+empirical artifacts, not just the branch's own. Deployed into run 0d0c3560 over nREPL.

title: Only prolog and z3 put the reviewer's objection in the shared failure log
description:
vf-i26 was fixed for verify and verify_smt and left half-done. verify_octave, verify_template, verify_lean and the new measure tool all record a GENERIC reason in the shared failure log: 'the Octave expression does not answer the claim', 'the template's slots do not match the claim'. The objection reaches the branch that made the mistake and dies there.

Observed cost in run 0d0c3560: four separate branches (B2 t5, B4.2.2 t30, B4.3 t29, and B2 t16 in a variant) independently wrote a counter over FEASIBLE flows and claimed it counted L1-OPTIMAL flows, dropping the cost-minimality constraint. The faithfulness judge caught every one and named the fix each time. The failure log — which exists precisely so branches do not repeat each other's dead ends — carried none of it.

Fix: thread the objection into :failure :reason on every path that has one, matching what verify and verify_smt already do.
acceptance_criteria: Every verify_* tool that rejects an artifact as unfaithful records the reviewer's objection, not a generic string, in the shared failure log.
close_reason: Closed

title: A tooling diagnostic can be confirmed, congratulated, and shared to every branch
description:
Live in run 0d0c3560 at turn 4: B3 verified 'Diagnostic: between(-1,1,X) succeeds for X = -1,0,1.', the engine said yes, the harness recorded a CONFIRMED artifact, the milestone gate congratulated it, and with HARNESS_SHARE_ARTIFACTS on it propagated into B1, B2 and B4's context as a shared confirmed result. Nothing about the problem had been established.

This is the exact zebra-run failure advances-thesis? was written for. The guard was inert because B3 had not registered a thesis, and with no thesis the function returns true for any claim — reasonable when the only consumer was the stall counter, wrong now that it is the only relevance signal in the system.

Three consequences, in increasing severity: the stall counter credits it as progress; the milestone and branch-out gates fire on it; and the shared pool exports it to every other branch, which is new with the sharing flag and is how one branch's tooling check becomes four branches' context.

Fix: when no thesis is registered, fall back to the branch's problem statement rather than returning true, and gate entry to the shared pool on the same predicate.
acceptance_criteria: A confirmed claim sharing no substantive vocabulary with the thesis OR the problem does not count as progress, does not fire the milestone or branch-out gates, and does not enter the shared artifact pool.
close_reason: Closed

title: Empirical work cannot be banked, so branches doing it get culled
description:
The phase-unwrap run made 84 octave_eval calls and banked zero artifacts from them. The branch whose thesis was 'empirically locate sigma_MCF' was culled at turn 12 with 0 confirmed artifacts, having done most of that simulation.

The critic scores branches on confirmed artifacts. The only way to bank one is a verify_* call needing a decidable claim, and verify_octave specifically wants one scalar boolean. A sweep that establishes 'recovery breaks around sigma 0.7, and the failure mode is path degeneracy' is the most valuable output available and is not a scalar boolean, so it scores nothing.

Consequence: the beam selects for whatever is easiest to state as a verifiable proposition, which was lemmas about 4-vertex graphs, and against the work that addresses the actual question. 129 of 206 turns went to octave_eval and lean_search that banked nothing.

Two possible fixes: a tool for recording a measurement as evidence (n, parameters, trial count, outcome), or prompt guidance that measurements must be phrased as bankable inequalities on computed counters. The second needs no code.
acceptance_criteria: A branch that measures something real can bank it and score for it.
close_reason: Closed

title: done gate checks evidential support but not relevance to the problem
description:
A branch shipped 'on the 4-cycle with oriented edges e0..e3 ... this refutes the claimed uniqueness lemma' as the final answer to 'when can 2D phase unwrapping be done exactly, and by a polynomial-time algorithm?'. The answer contains no phase field, no noise parameter, no torus, no threshold and no algorithm.

Both gates behaved correctly by their own criteria. The LLM audit passed with 'GAPS: none'. The done gate's uncovered-tokens check verified every substantive token appears in a confirmed artifact — which it does, because the answer IS a confirmed artifact verbatim.

Nothing checks that the answer addresses the problem statement. Same shape as gen-15 shipping a corollary of Balister et al as its final answer.

state.clj already has advances-thesis? for exactly this reason (a run once verified 'clpfd is available' and the milestone gate congratulated it). That guard protects milestones; nothing equivalent guards done.
acceptance_criteria: An answer that does not engage with the problem statement is refused, or the refusal names what it fails to address.
close_reason: Closed

title: An unfaithful prolog artifact was reported to the branch as a success
description:
The prolog verify path set claim-status :unfaithful but left :category :success, :progress? true, and a result string reading 'The goal succeeded with N solution(s)'. The structural objection was journalled and shown to nobody.

Caught live: a branch posted clpfd constraints inside \+ on turn 25, the deterministic check fired, the artifact was marked unfaithful — and the branch was told the goal succeeded, so it repeated the identical defect on turn 26. Two turns burned with no way for the model to learn.

verify_smt, verify_octave and verify_lean all explain an :unfaithful outcome. The prolog path never did; the status was added without the reporting.

Fixed: the structural check is hoisted so its warnings can be quoted back to the branch, an unfaithful outcome now reports :failure with progress? false, and the result carries the objection text plus 'restating the claim to match a goal that enforces nothing is not a fix'.
acceptance_criteria: An unfaithful prolog artifact returns category :failure, scores no progress, and its result names the defect.
close_reason: Fixed and hot-reloaded into the live run over nREPL without restarting it. Test: an-unfaithful-prolog-artifact-is-reported-as-a-failure-with-the-reason.

title: Branch panel hangs forever on any large branch
description:
branch-detail called journal/turns, which SELECTs every turn of the whole run with every column, then filtered for one branch in Clojure. So every branch click paid a 5.8MB whole-run fetch (gen-14) regardless of branch size, with 5.5MB of it assistant_text that no display path reads. Measured on the live server: 6-turn branches 2.6-4.5s, a 51-turn branch >50s. The GUI's socket timeout is 45s, so large branches never loaded.

Worse, the client discarded the failure: refresh-branch-log! only swapped state on (:ok r), so a timeout left :branch-log nil and the panel read '(loading full turn results and encodings...)' forever, with no way to tell a slow fetch from a dead one. The poll loop then refired it on every event touching the branch, queueing a fresh doomed 45s request about once a second. Same shape as the crashed-run-still-marked-running bug.

Also fixed alongside: the poll loop compared the selected NODE id against event branch_ids, but an artifact node's id is '<branch>@<turn>', so artifact panels never refreshed at all.
acceptance_criteria: A branch with 50+ turns loads its panel, and a failed fetch says so instead of showing a permanent loading line.
close_reason: journal/branch-turns filters by branch in SQL (using the idx_turns_run index, which was going unused) and drops assistant_text/reasoning_text from the projection — 5,857,814 bytes to 69,366, an 84x reduction. journal/turns keeps its full-row shape because resume replays assistant_text from it. Client side: refresh-branch-log! now records the failure in :branch-log-error and the panel says why it is missing, noting the live activity and attempts above it are complete; and the poll loop compares against selected-branch-id so artifact panels refresh too. Tests: branch-turns-reads-one-branch-and-leaves-the-bulk-behind.

title: Judge verdicts are unattributable — reasoning is never journalled
description:
A faithfulness rejection leaves claim-status = unfaithful and nothing else. The judge's answer, the gap it named and its reasoning are all discarded, so there is no way to tell a caught defect from a misfire.

Hit for real on gen-14 turn 10: a#350 (octave, mod-105 slack enumeration for {3,5,7,11}) was rejected as unfaithful. Its arithmetic is independently confirmed correct — all eight scaled constants and the minimum -647 at (1,1,2,4) reproduce exactly — so either the reviewer caught a framing defect (the claim names four residues but the encoding also fixes a3=a5=a7=0 by translation symmetry, undisclosed) or it misfired on the abandoned glpk scratch block the workspace log now carries. The journal cannot distinguish them.

This blocks the question that decides whether the whole faithfulness gate is worth having: what is its false-positive rate on real work.

Also note: only rejections being visible would bias the answer, so passes must be recorded too, and a transport failure that fails closed must be distinguishable from a rejection on the merits.
acceptance_criteria: Every judge call records its label, verdict, named gaps and reasoning in the journal, for passes and failures alike.
close_reason:
Fixed in 8de8632: note-verdict! inside judge/2 records label, verdict, named gaps, prompt size and the answer (reasoning stripped, capped at 4000 chars) for every judge call — faithfulness, review and audit alike, passes as well as failures, with transport failures distinguishable from rejections on the merits. Tests: a-judge-verdict-is-journalled-with-its-reasoning, a-judge-verdict-that-passes-is-journalled-too.

The motivating question is now answered, offline, by reconstructing the prompt: the judge was RIGHT both times. Its gap on a#350 — 'the claim is for support {3,5,7,11}, but the artifact never uses the prime 11' — is correct, since 11 is coprime to 105 and enters the argument only through the eight scaled constants, which neither artifact derives. Not deployed: needs a jolt serve restart, which would end gen-14.

title: Faithfulness checks don't cover lean, octave, template, or refutations
description:
After a701e51, verify_smt and verify (prolog) run deterministic structural checks then the LLM judge. Still uncovered:

1. verify_lean, verify_octave, verify_template have neither layer. gen-13 a#344 is a confirmed artifact whose entire evidence is a glpk floating-point value (1.014488 > 1, self-declared tolerance 0.001) with nothing comparing computation to claim. Its conclusion happened to be correct and separately proved exactly, so nothing rested on it — but a numeric artifact with a hand-stated tolerance was recorded as engine-confirmed unexamined.

2. REFUTATIONS skip both layers, since the checks run only on would-be confirmations. gen-13 a#336 recorded a refutation whose claim asserted unrestricted domains while its encoding pinned y0 = 0. A refuted artifact asserts the negation, which is still a fact entering the run's record and readable by other branches.

3. Known limitation of the count check, pinned by test: a claim stating FEWER constraints than the encoding asserts is undetectable, because a surplus is what correct artifacts look like (bounds, symmetry breaks). gen-12's a#321/a#324 said '14 inequalities' over 15. Catching that needs identifying which asserts are class constraints, or a claim-internal consistency check (the claim listed three families of 3, 5 and 7).

Suggested order: extend the structural+judge pair to octave first (numeric claims are the least self-evidencing), then refutations, then lean/template.
acceptance_criteria: A confirmed octave/lean/template artifact and a refutation both face the same checks verify_smt does.
close_reason: Octave, Lean and verify_template now run structural checks then the judge, and refutations face both layers. New deterministic checks: octave expressions that compute nothing (a#344), unsat over an undisclosed partial family pin (a#336), and claims whose enumerated index families exceed their stated total (a#321/a#324, the case the assert count could not reach). Validated against all 348 artifacts in the journal: 1 of 42 octave rows objected to, 1 of 108 smt rows, 2 of 348 claims — every one a known-bad artifact, zero false positives. Also fixed: a Lean snippet the REPL rejects no longer records a :refuted artifact, and verify_template no longer claims its cross-check makes review unnecessary.

title: Faithfulness check can be satisfied by weakening the claim, not fixing the encoding
description:
The vf-slr faithfulness judge compares claim to encoding and passes when they agree. Agreement can be reached from either end, and restating the claim is far cheaper than fixing the formula — so the check creates an incentive to drift the claim down onto whatever was encoded.

Observed live in gen-12 (run 98d0423e), branch B2, within four turns:

  a#318  p=5 base 662, 135 wrongly counted coprime to 5, no assignable 135 term  -> PASSED (miss)
  a#319  base corrected to 655, 135 still absent                                 -> blocked (correct)
  a#320  regressed to 662                                                        -> blocked (correct)
  a#321  same defective encoding as a#320, CLAIM REWRITTEN to transcribe it      -> CONFIRMED

a#321's claim now reads 'there is no assignment ... such that ALL of the following 14 inequalities hold: ... 662 + sum over m in {5,15,35,45,105,315,945} ...'. It spells out the wrong base and the omitted modulus as the content of the claim. The encoding is genuinely faithful to that claim and Z3's unsat genuinely establishes it, so the judge was right to pass it. The artifact is true and establishes nothing about covering systems.

Two things to fix:

1. tools.clj run-tool verify_smt result text for :unfaithful literally instructs this: 'or restate the claim to match what you encoded'. Drop that half of the sentence.

2. The check needs a relevance leg, not just a consistency leg. Candidates: judge the claim against the branch's pinned thesis rather than only against the encoding; or reject claims that are transcriptions of their own formula (a claim naming explicit coefficient lists is describing an artifact, not a theorem).

Also worth a cheap deterministic pre-check that needs no LLM: for any claim naming a layered condition mod p, verify the coprime base equals sum of L/m over {m in support : p does not divide m}, and that every m with p|m appears as an assignable term. That arithmetic would have caught a#318, a#319, a#320 and a#321 without a model call.
acceptance_criteria: A branch cannot get a confirmation by restating the claim to match a defective encoding; the misleading half of the :unfaithful message is gone.
close_reason: Fixed across 965b459 and a701e51. The 'or restate the claim to match what you encoded' escape is gone from the :unfaithful message. More importantly the drift incentive is largely removed: the deterministic checks in agent.faithful cannot be argued with, so rewriting the claim no longer buys a confirmation past a bad coefficient or a missing constraint. Known limitation, pinned by test: a claim stating FEWER constraints than the encoding asserts (gen-12's 14-vs-15) is not detectable, since a surplus of asserts is what correct artifacts look like.

title: A shipped branch is never closed in the run record
description:
tools/done sets :status :done and :final-answer. Both DB-close paths in beam/run-loop miss that combination: the post-cull loop writes only branches with (not (:final-answer b)), and the run-end done-branch loop writes only (state/active? b) ones. So a branch that ships keeps status='active' in the branches table forever and never emits a branch-closed event.

Seen in gen-10 (05ecb88a): the run completed with all nine surviving branches shipped, and all nine still read 'active'. The GUI folds status from branch-closed events, so a finished run renders nine live branches, and the working indicator keys on :active too. Their engines are also held to run end instead of being disposed when the branch stops working.
close_reason: Closed

description: UCLA Track B: when nothing ships, emit an honest structured progress report instead of a failure string - never ship nothing, never ship a lie. Extends the planned residual-objectives item: on beam exhaustion assemble per-branch undischarged thesis sub-claims, best confirmed artifacts with provenance, top shared-failure-log entries, and gate history summary, explicitly labeled not-a-solution. Do-not-claim-more-than-proved is mechanical for us: only engine-confirmed artifacts appear as established.

title: Wind-down arbiter rung at late turn budget
description: UCLA reserves a deadline tail exclusively for assembly and shipping. Our 85% turn-budget notice informs but does not steer. Add an arbiter rung: at the late notice, the steer becomes assemble-and-ship-what-you-have (today only a human intervention example). Declares a prediction like other gates (branch calls audit or review within N turns) settled from the journal; sits below human directives and done-block in priority; one-shot re-fire guard.

title: Audit restatement and is-relaxation axis
description: Audit must restate, self-contained, what the answer actually establishes (no anaphora), plus an is-relaxation flag comparing that against the pinned thesis - a failed attempt at the full claim is NOT a relaxation. Unlike UCLA we never re-pin the claim to the restatement (their ratchet let proofs pass against shrunken claims); drift is recorded against the original thesis. Claim-evidence gate extended: an artifact confirming only a weakened claim cannot substantiate the full answer, generalizing the existential bucket.
acceptance_criteria: Audit output schema carries restatement + is-relaxation. Anti-conflation rule in prompt. Thesis stays pinned; drift journaled. Claim-evidence gate refuses relaxation-only coverage; scripted transcript proves it. Existential-bucket tests still pass.
close_reason: ESTABLISHED/RELAXATION parsing, thesis-drift journal, done-gate relaxation refusal; 98 tests green

title: Named exemption lists in audit/review prompts
description: UCLA strictness was usable only because routine facts are exempted by name with DO-NOT-FLAG lists; without them the referee drowns everything in nitpicks and burns the done-block budget on non-gaps. Add named exemption lists to our audit/review prompt files (routine algebraic steps, standard library lemmas already engine-confirmed, phrasing/exposition items). Measure by max-done-blocks firings before/after on the probe set; the false-positive probe must still refuse.
acceptance_criteria: Exemption lists in prompt files as data-like sections. Probe set unchanged results for real gaps (false-positive probe still refuses; claim-evidence transcript still blocks). Bench note comparing done-block firings.

title: Judge-not-vote contract for verdict aggregation
description: Encode the UCLA consensus judge principle as a mechanical contract wherever more than one verdict about the same claim exists: LLM verdicts are evidence, never votes - no code path may majority-count them. Counting is legitimate only for independent engine confirmations (Prolog/Z3/Lean agreeing), which compose empirically. If multiple review/audit verdicts are ever aggregated, aggregation goes through a single judge that must record per-disagreement reasoning in the journal. Ship the contract and tests now so any future multi-model review lands inside it.
acceptance_criteria: A verdict-aggregation namespace with the contract in its docstring. Tests: aggregating N LLM verdicts by count throws or is unrepresentable; engine-confirmation counting allowed; judge path records reasoning per disagreement. Gate table untouched.
close_reason: consensus namespace + judge prompt + 7 contract tests; 89 tests green

title: Patch-existence severity criterion in audit/review
description: UCLA scorer_v4 core idea: a gap is BLOCKING only if the verifier cannot supply the concrete fix; if it can, the fix text must be included and the gap is minor - severity becomes operationally checkable and the refusal doubles as repair input. Apply to audit/review prompts: verdicts carry a gap list where each minor gap must embed its patch; done-refusal messages carry the patches so a refused turn is spent on repair, not re-diagnosis. Composes with max-done-blocks (each refusal costs a turn).
acceptance_criteria: Audit/review prompts restructured with MAJOR-iff-no-concrete-fix rule and mandatory patch text on minor gaps. verdict.clj parses gap+patch structure. done-refusal steer includes patches verbatim. Tests with corpus phrasings; probe transcript where a patchable gap does not block done but an unpatchable one does.
close_reason: MINOR/FIX parsing, fold-to-blocking rule, third disagreement direction, PATCHES in refusals; 91 tests green

title: Harden constrained-verdict contract in verdict.clj

They independently abandoned a 1-10 score for a 3-class enum with fail-closed parsing, converging on our design; their additions we lack: (a) an anti-contradiction instruction in the audit/review prompts (a verdict of pass alongside a listed blocking gap is self-contradictory - pick the worse verdict), (b) a disagreement signal computed from the response text when the verdict line conflicts with the gap list, journaled like the auto-repaired signal rather than silently reconciled, with the verdict winning. Keep :unparseable failing closed.

title: The nREPL listen socket is inherited by every engine subprocess
description:
Twin of vf-k0a, on the socket that fix did not cover. lsof against the live server:

  jolt   46865  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47093  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47095  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47097  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47099  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)

Four swipl, one per branch in gen-19's beam, all holding the nREPL listener on fd 10. Port 3985 was clean, because vf-k0a's fix covers the vendored ring adapter only — this socket is created by jolt.nrepl in jolt core, with the same raw FFI socket/bind/listen and no close-on-exec.

Consequence is the same and it bites the workflow this project depends on: the port stays bound while any engine subprocess lives, so killing the server leaves the next start unable to bind its nREPL — which is the one channel for patching a live run without restarting it.

FIXED in jolt, branch fix/nrepl-socket-cloexec (58e0cc8b), pushed and awaiting a PR: SOCK_CLOEXEC on Linux, fcntl F_SETFD elsewhere on POSIX (bound with :varargs, since a fixed-arity fcntl corrupts the stack-passed argument on Apple arm64), and neither on Windows, which uses HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT. Verified by spawning a sleep beside a live nREPL and listing the port's holders: only the jolt process, where the same probe previously showed the child too. jolt unit suite clean.

NOT yet in effect here: veriframe runs the installed jolt 0.7.6, which predates this. The running server still shows the four swipl.
acceptance_criteria: lsof on a running veriframe server with a warm beam shows only jolt holding the nREPL port.

title: gen-17 and gen-18 have no write-up
description:
The prior generation produced docs/phase-unwrapping.md. gen-17 (0d0c3560, 523 turns, 97 artifacts, 56 confirmed, 10 branches shipped) and gen-18 (65d50333, 603 turns, died ~20h in) have had none, so the three-stage canonical rule and everything gen-18 established about it exist only in the journal and in this session's notes.

Should cover at least:

Stage 2 works because a Q level set lies inside a sphere in Z^E and is finite, collapsing the unbounded L1 argmin. The argument holds for real nonnegative weights, which is stronger than the natural-valued Lean version.

title: close() did not release the listen port on Linux
description:
Found because the FD_CLOEXEC guard (vf-k0a) asserted the flag separately from its consequence. On CI the flag WAS set and the port still could not be rebound, which ruled out fd inheritance and pointed at shutdown.

stop-server set running? false and called close() on the listen fd. close() does not reliably wake a thread already blocked in accept(): macOS wakes it, Linux does not, so the accept thread kept the socket alive and the port stayed bound after stop-server returned. Next bind got address-in-use — the same symptom vf-k0a described, from an unrelated cause, which is exactly why the single-assertion version of that test was unreadable when it failed.

The adapter's own comment asserted the macOS behaviour as general: 'stop-server closes the listen fd (which unblocks accept)'.

FIXED: shutdown(fd, SHUT_RDWR) before close(). ENOTCONN from a listening socket on macOS is expected and ignored. Covered by the rebind half of server_test/a-subprocess-does-not-inherit-the-listen-socket; CI green on all four jobs including the Lean suite.
close_reason: Fixed by shutdown() before close() in vendor/ring_chez/adapter.clj; CI green on all four jobs.

title: Lean subprocesses inherit the server's listening socket
description:
lsof against a running jolt serve shows the HTTP listening socket held by three processes, on the same fd and the same kernel object:

  jolt  97090  4u  IPv4 0xb9638a5d078eee09  TCP 127.0.0.1:3985 (LISTEN)
  lake  97125  4u  IPv4 0xb9638a5d078eee09  TCP 127.0.0.1:3985 (LISTEN)
  repl  97149  4u  IPv4 0xb9638a5d078eee09  TCP 127.0.0.1:3985 (LISTEN)

lake/repl are the Lean pool's children (engine/lean-repl spawns lake env <repl-bin>). They inherited fd 4 because it is not marked close-on-exec.

Why it matters: the port stays bound as long as ANY holder is alive. Kill the server while a Lean session lingers — which is exactly what happens when a run is abandoned, since the repl is a long-lived process spawned with p/destroy-tree as a shutdown hook rather than a guarantee — and a restart fails with address-in-use against a server that is no longer running. The listener is also reachable by a subprocess that has no business holding it.

Applies to every subprocess the harness spawns, not just Lean: prolog and octave take the same path.

Fix is either O_CLOEXEC on the listening socket where it is created, or an explicit close in the child between fork and exec. Which one depends on what jolt.process exposes.
close_reason: Fixed in vendor/ring_chez/adapter.clj: close-on-exec! marks the listen fd and every accepted connection with FD_CLOEXEC via a :varargs fcntl binding (SOCK_CLOEXEC is Linux-only). Covered by server_test/a-subprocess-does-not-inherit-the-listen-socket, which spawns a child, stops the server and rebinds — red before (bind() failed on port 39187), green after. Verified live: lsof on a running server now shows only jolt on 3985, with the Lean repl warm and Mathlib imported.

title: The gl-area pointer goes stale while the widget is being replaced
description:
CORRECTED 2026-08-12 after looking at the full log rather than its tail.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS. glpane caches the widget as a raw pointer in st (:area, written only by on-realize). When the widget is destroyed and rebuilt, every request-render! between the destroy and the new on-realize hits freed memory, and GTK answers:

  Gtk-CRITICAL gtk_gl_area_queue_render: assertion 'GTK_IS_GL_AREA (area)' failed

Timestamps from one session — 15 criticals, not a steady stream:
  23:21:45 .. 23:22:13   13 of them, ~2.4s apart (the poll interval)
  (nothing for ten minutes)
  23:32:16, 23:32:25     2 more, exactly when start-run probes added runs

So it is a TRANSIENT window during widget replacement, and the pane RECOVERS when the replacement realizes. My original filing said the pane 'never repaints again' — that was wrong, inferred from a tail that happened to catch the burst. Severity is log noise plus a few dropped repaints, not a dead pane.

WHAT WAS FIXED. root renders a tree with no :gl-area in it while :composing? is true, so opening the new-run form genuinely destroys the pane. glpane/unmount! now clears the cached pointer and the GL object names, and toggle-compose! calls it on the way in; closing the form mounts a fresh area whose on-realize repopulates them. The misleading comment in root claiming the pane 'keeps its context' while the form is open is corrected.

WHAT IS NOT FIXED — the path that produced the criticals above. Neither burst came from the compose toggle: the first is at startup and the second coincides with runs appearing in the list. Both are re-render churn — root derefs @state and rebuilds the whole tree, and the :gl-area child is evidently being replaced rather than preserved, despite graph-pane being deref-free for exactly that reason. The real fix is either stable reconciliation for that child (a glimmer concern) or not caching a raw widget pointer across renders at all. Needs someone who can watch the window while toggling and selecting.

NOT COVERED BY A TEST. glpane requires glimmer-gl.gtk, so the headless suite cannot load it; nothing in test/ references glpane. The unmount! change is verified by reading, not by execution.
acceptance_criteria: No GTK_IS_GL_AREA assertion in the GUI log during a normal session, and the pane visibly repaints after a run is selected and after the poll loop updates.
notes: 2026-08-12 second pass. Compose-toggle destroy path fixed (glpane/unmount!). The observed bursts are NOT from that path, so the bug stays open — but realize! now detects and prints when it is handed a different area than the one cached, which is exactly the widget-replacement event. Next GUI session that produces the GTK critical will also produce a line naming it, turning an inferred cause into a recorded one.
close_reason:
Fixed at the mechanism rather than by enumerating the ways a widget can die. glpane now connects to the gl-area's own GTK 'unrealize' signal via glimmer.ffi/g-signal-connect-data and clears the cached pointer and GL objects when it fires; realize! puts them back. That covers every teardown — the new-run form (which renders a tree with no :gl-area), glimmer's positional reconciler destroying a child when a slot's tag changes, and reparenting — without needing a hook glimmer does not have. The callable is retained, since a collected one leaves GTK holding a dangling function pointer, and each widget is wired once.

Verified: handler id came back 404 (nonzero — an invalid signal name returns 0 and warns), no gsignal warning, and a 60s GUI session against a live run produced an entirely empty log where the same window previously produced a 13-critical burst. The replacement-detection println is kept as a backstop, since the only evidence this bug ever gave was a GTK critical with nothing naming the transition.

title: A Lean import line cost 19 turns across two runs
description:

Counted across the two phase-unwrapping runs: 19 turns. gen-18 alone hit it on 7 branches (B2, B2.3.3, B2.3.3.3 x2, B3 x2, B4.3 x5, B4.3.3 x2, B4.3.3.2). B3 spent two of the six failures that culled it on this, while pursuing the convex-cost-flow reduction.

strip-lean-imports now drops import lines in lean-repl/run-command, which covers every caller. open lines are left alone since they are legal against an existing env, and a line merely mentioning the word is untouched.
acceptance_criteria: A snippet with a leading import runs instead of erroring; open lines and identifiers containing 'import' survive.

title: B2's Q-A class excludes the tied-path mechanism, and the answer does not say so
description:
gen-18 B2 (run 65d50333, T62) settled Q-A for instances with a UNIQUE stage-2 minimizer. The algorithm and correctness proof are right — I verified the scalarization, the [-D,D] bound, and the outside-the-box argument independently.

But the restriction excludes the tied-path mechanism entirely:
  3x3 grid, 9 L1-minimizers, Q = [6,6,6,6,6,6,8,8,10] — six tie at the minimum
  one dipole gadget, 2 minimizers, both Q=2
  m gadgets, 2^m minimizers, all Q=2m
  5-vertex zero-weight cycle — stage-2 minimizer IS unique, so this one is covered

Stage 2 collapses infinite ambiguity and does nothing about combinatorial ambiguity. The open part of Q-A is therefore exactly stage 3: lexicographic selection over a Q-tied set.

The answer states the restriction in its first sentence but never says which established instances fall outside it, and every reader of this campaign would want that.
acceptance_criteria: The write-up states which of the campaign's own instances are outside B2's class, and gen-19's formulation targets stage 3 over a Q-tied set as the remaining open part of Q-A.
notes: Taken up by gen-19 (cd58e618, launched 2026-08-13, seeded from gen-18, beam 4, 300 turns). The formulation makes this gap the MAIN question: Q-1 asks for a polynomial-time algorithm without assuming a unique stage-2 minimizer, which forces stage 3 over a possibly exponential set, and names the crux — whether the lexicographically least element of the stage-2 set can be found without enumerating it. Q-2 asks whether stage 3 is even the right tie-break, since it depends on edge ordering rather than on the instance. Q-3 asks how big the tie actually gets on grid instances rather than adversarial gadgets. Also documented in docs/phase-unwrapping-2.md.

title: Clean turns did not work off the cull budget
description:
consecutive-failures was cleared only by :success, which in practice means banking an artifact. A branch that hit a rough patch and then worked productively still carried the stale count into the cull gate.

gen-18 B1 made three malformed tool calls, then three clean Octave runs producing dual potentials, and was culled on a counter last incremented three turns before. The guard against well-formed but useless calls is turns-since-progress, which a neutral turn still increments, so decaying the failure count on a clean turn gives nothing away.
acceptance_criteria: A neutral turn decrements consecutive-failures, floored at zero; sustained failure still outpaces recovery.
close_reason: Fixed, tested, deployed into run 65d50333 over nREPL.

title: Repopulation is an invitation with no prediction, declined 9 times in 12
description:
Run 0d0c3560, first 120 turns: 12 repopulate invitations, 3 accepted. Every acceptance came when the beam was already collapsing (B4 declined twice at alive=3 and accepted at alive=1). The current phase is 5 consecutive declines at alive=3, one every turn or two, rotating across branches because the cooldown is per-branch.

Two problems, neither of them 'repopulation does not work' — it does, and all four of this run's forks came from it.

First, it is an invitation, not a gate. It appends a message directly in the scheduler instead of going through the arbiter, so it carries no prediction, settles nothing, and appears in no gate tally. The decline rate was invisible until someone counted branch-opened events by hand. This is the exact reasoning that turned branch-out from an invitation into a gate: 'an invitation the model may decline is not a mechanism; a gate with a settled prediction is.' Repopulation was left behind.

Second, being outside the arbiter it is a second harness voice on the same boundary as whatever gate fired, so 'at most one steer per boundary' holds for gates only.

Fix: make it a gate. The precondition needs facts only the scheduler has (alive count, target, which branch is strongest), so the scheduler should mark the chosen branch and the gate should read the mark.
acceptance_criteria: A repopulation ask is recorded as a gate firing with a prediction, settles met or unmet like every other gate, and cannot land on the same boundary as another steer.
close_reason: Repopulation is now the :repopulate gate (priority 6, above branch-out): the scheduler marks the strongest survivor and the gate does the asking, so it carries a prediction, settles met/unmet on branch_theses, appears in the gate tally, and cannot land on a boundary that already had a steer. Budget :max-repopulates. Covered by agent_test/repopulation-is-a-gate-with-a-prediction-not-an-invitation.

title: Enumerate and close the finite sub-257 four-prime supports
description:
Finding 11 (gen-15) proved every density-feasible four-prime support outside the three dense base triples {3,5,7}, {3,5,11}, {3,5,13} has all primes < 257, and the bound is sharp ({3,5,17,251} is feasible at 2.000156). That list is finite and has never been enumerated, let alone closed.

Enumerate them explicitly, then close each with the per-class LP at whichever Q divides the support. With the sibling families this completes the four-prime tier.
acceptance_criteria: The finite list is enumerated with a stated count, and each member is closed or explicitly left open with a reason.

title: Close the two remaining four-prime families with the per-class LP
description:
Finding 12 closed {3,5,7,11} and with it all {3,5,7,q}, using the per-class assignment LP instead of the M_g bound. The same method is UNTRIED on the two sibling families.

By monotonicity in the fourth prime, each family reduces to its smallest member:
- {3,5,11,q} -> {3,5,7,11} at Q=165. Old M_g bound there: -2303/480.
- {3,5,13,q} -> {3,5,7,13} at Q=195. Old M_g bound there: -1729/576.

Both are exactly the situation at Q=105, where M_g gave -647/480 and the LP was infeasible for all 9,835 orbits. Method: fix the unit-weight residues (WLOG the prime ones to 0 by translation), derive F1 and A_g from P, build the LP with y_{g,b} >= 0, sum_b y_{g,b} <= A_g, every uncovered class needing 1-F1, and sweep orbits under multiplication by units mod Q (order phi(165)=80, phi(195)=96).

Closing both, plus the finite list below, gives 'every odd covering system needs at least five distinct odd primes'.
acceptance_criteria: The per-class LP is checked over all orbit representatives at Q=165 and Q=195, with the orbit count stated and the constants derived from P.

title: Retry a __no_call__ turn with a doubled budget
description:
A branch that spends its whole output budget reasoning and never emits a tool call is a process failure, not evidence - the same thing vf-mti fixed for the judge, on the branch loop instead. Currently the turn is scored a failure, the harness appends 'Think less and call a tool', and the branch loses the turn.

Seen on gen-11 (90336412) turn 1: all three branches produced 48-51k characters, hit the 16384 cap, and called nothing. It self-corrects once conversation history exists (turn 3 was down to 4.7k), so the cost is a first-turn tax that scales with how dense the seeded brief is - and the brief gets denser every generation.

Fix: on __no_call__, retry once inside the same turn with a doubled max-tokens, journalled like judge-retry. Reuse the arithmetic-heavy sizing from tools/judge-max-tokens so a brief full of exact rationals opens high instead of paying for the doomed call first.
close_reason: Fixed in a701e51: call-model retries once at a doubled budget when the response hit the token cap before emitting a tool call. Bounded to one retry; truncation that still carried a call is not retried. Journalled as :turn-retry.

title: Start a new run from the GUI

title: Size the judge's token budget to the claim, not retry into it
description:
Measured on gen-10 (05ecb88a): audit/review are the beam's critical path. In rounds of width>=7 they were the straggler 24 of 28 times while taking ~24% of turns; verify_lean gated a round once in 47 turns and verify_smt never. 39 of the run's 46 judge-retries land after turn 40, when claims became exact-rational assertions over 20-26 moduli. The judge burns its output budget re-checking the arithmetic, hits the cap with no verdict, and is retried at doubled max-tokens - so an arithmetic-heavy audit costs 2-3 calls.

Fix: estimate the needed budget up front (claim length, count of rational literals / large denominators) and open the audit at the higher cap when it looks arithmetic-heavy, keeping retry as the fallback rather than the norm. Should cut the tail that sets round wall-clock while the other branches sit at the advance-all barrier.
close_reason: Closed

Second branch reaching the same claim waits or receives existing confirmed artifact with provenance rather than respending provider tokens.

title: The abort endpoint answers 200 with an error body for a run that is not active
description:
POST /v1/runs/<id>/abort returns HTTP 200 with {"error":"no active run <id>"} when the run is already finished or was never in the in-memory active map. Observed while cleaning up probe runs:

  $ curl -X POST .../v1/runs/7dc1d22c-.../abort -w '%{http_code}'
  {"error":"no active run 7dc1d22c-4827-4e2f-96d6-13690b9aaaad"}
  200

A caller checking the status code alone reads that as a successful abort. Nothing in the GUI does — api/abort! hands the body back and the caller renders it — so this is not currently biting.

Flagged rather than changed because the same shape is deliberate elsewhere: start-run! documents that it answers 200 with an {:error ...} body when the beam does not come up, and gui.api/start-run! exists partly to fold exactly that case. So 200-plus-error-body may be this API's house style rather than a defect, and making abort a 404 alone would leave the two inconsistent in the other direction. Wants a decision about the convention, not a one-line change.
close_reason:
Both deviations brought onto the API's existing convention — a real status plus {:error {:message ...}}, which is what 'no such run', 'no such branch', the 404 fallback, the 500 handler and resume's 409 already did. abort on a non-active run is now 409 (matching resume's 'not resumable': the run exists, it is just not in an abortable state); a start that does not come up in 30s is 503 (the request was fine, the server could not service it).

Both now use resume's envelope — success {:body ...}, refusal {:status N :body ...} — so one route shape serves both. That envelope is load-bearing: the abort success body carries :status "aborting", the RUN's state, and a route reading (:status r) off a bare map would have sent the string "aborting" as the HTTP status. My first attempt did exactly that and the test caught it.

Verified live over nREPL without restarting: POST /v1/runs/no-such-run/abort returns 409 with {"error":{"message":"no active run ..."},"run_id":"..."}.

title: start-run! documents itself as immediate but waits for the whole beam
description:
api.control/start-run! says 'Kick off a run in the background and return its id immediately.' It does not. It blocks on (deref promised 30000), and beam/run! only calls on-start after opening every branch:

  run-id (runs/start-run! conn {...})        ; row committed
  _ (when seed-run (artifacts/seed-from-run! ...))
  initial (mapv #(open-branch! ctx ...) (range width))
  (when on-start (on-start run-id))          ; response released here

So POST /v1/runs takes as long as opening the whole beam. Measured 47ms idle and 21095ms moments later under load, with beam_width 1; a wider beam opens proportionally more branches first.

This is what made vf-36o possible: any client bound tighter than 30s reports a failure for a run that is committed and running. That was fixed on the client, which is correct but treats the symptom.

Moving on-start to just after the row insert would make the docstring true and the endpoint fast and predictable. The cost is handing out an id for a run whose branches do not exist yet, so a client that immediately fetches run-detail sees zero branches — the poller tolerates that, but anything asserting on branch count would need checking first. Not done here because it changes the run lifecycle rather than a timeout, and deserves a deliberate call.
close_reason: on-start now fires before the beam opens its branches, so POST /v1/runs returns as soon as the run row exists rather than after a Prolog session is spawned per branch. Covered by agent_test/on-start-fires-before-the-beam-opens-its-branches.

title: Two dead runs are still marked running in the DB
description:
runs.status is 'running' for 65d50333-1751-402d-a200-cd4f287b78d5 (gen-18) and 90336412-b135-422c-a9cf-116064890e12 (gen-11), but neither has a process. gen-18's server died around 2026-08-10 20:15 (last DB write) roughly 20 hours into a max_turns=300 beam-4 run; ended_at is NULL for both.

SUPERSEDES vf-60k, which filed the gen-11 row alone. I filed this one without noticing that, so the two are the same defect seen twice — which is itself the argument for fixing the mechanism rather than the rows: this will keep recurring once per crash.

Not silently wrong — the API computes :stalled from last_progress_at and reports true for both, which is what that field is for — but the status column still lies and list-runs shows them as live.

NOT fixed here for two reasons. A direct sqlite UPDATE on veriframe.sqlite3 is blocked by the permission classifier and needs a human decision. And the right fix is probably not a one-off UPDATE anyway: something should reconcile 'running' rows with no live process at startup, so a crash does not leave the row asserting forever. Worth deciding which is wanted before touching data.
close_reason: Fixed at the mechanism rather than by correcting rows: system/start! calls runs/reconcile-orphans!, which marks every row still claiming to run as interrupted with an ended_at. Sound only at startup, which is when it runs, because the beam only ever runs in this process. Verified live — the server logged 'marked 2 run(s) interrupted' and both gen-18 (65d50333) and gen-11 (90336412) now read interrupted. Covered by store_test/a-run-left-running-by-a-crash-is-reconciled-at-startup.

title: B4 shipped a 12-vertex graph described as 16-vertex, and both gates agreed
description:
B4 of run 0d0c3560 shipped: 'For the 16-vertex/12-edge graph consisting of three disjoint two-path dipole gadgets...'. The construction in its own code builds s=4g+1, a=4g+2, b=4g+3, t=4g+4 for g=0,1,2 — vertices 1..12. The graph has TWELVE vertices. B4.2.2 describes the same object correctly as '12-vertex, 12-edge'.

The 16 comes from the code's own 'Nv = 16; A = zeros(Nv, Ne)'. Rows 13..16 are never assigned, so they stay zero, and the constraint A*x == b on them reads 0 == 0 and is satisfied by everything. The count of 8 and the cost of 6 are unaffected: the mathematics is right and the description is wrong.

Why neither gate caught it. The faithfulness judge asks whether the artifact formalises the claim; claim and code both say 16, so they agree. Nothing compares either to what the construction actually builds. The coverage rung asks whether a number in the answer appears in the evidence, and 16 does — in the mislabelled artifact. A number that is wrong consistently in both places passes both checks.

No fix proposed. This is a judge miss on a decorative constant rather than a structural hole, and inventing a mechanical check for 'does the prose vertex count match the edge list' is not worth it. Recorded so the number is not propagated, and so the write-up says twelve.
acceptance_criteria: The run write-up states the correct vertex count and notes that the shipped answer overstated it.
close_reason: Acceptance criteria met: docs/phase-unwrapping-2.md states the graph has twelve vertices, notes that gen-17's B4 shipped '16-vertex', and records why both gates passed it — claim and code agreed because the code's own Nv=16 left rows 13..16 all-zero, so the constraint on them read 0==0, and the coverage rung found 16 in the (mislabelled) evidence. The bead proposed no code fix by design: a mechanical 'does the prose vertex count match the edge list' check is not worth building for a decorative constant. Numbers unaffected — 8 flows at cost 6 both verified.

title: gen-11's run row still says running
description:
Run 90336412-b135-422c-a9cf-116064890e12 (generation 11) died without the supervisor noticing and its row still reads status='running'. It shows up in the run list and in any 'is anything active' check.

The abort endpoint cannot fix it: abort! only works on runs held in the in-memory 'active' map in api/control.clj, and this run predates every server restart since. It needs a direct UPDATE on veriframe.sqlite3, which the permission classifier blocked during the session where it was found. Left alone rather than worked around.

The underlying invisible-crash cause is fixed (run-error journalling plus runs/finish-run! :failed in beam/run-rounds); this is just the stale row.

title: Turn the {3,5,7,11} closure into an argument rather than 9,835 LP solves
description:
Finding 12 is a computation: 9,835 orbit LPs, all infeasible. A proof would be an explicit rule for the dual weights lambda_c -- some function of a class's residues, or of the sizes of the blocks it sits in -- shown to satisfy D*sum lambda_c > sum_g A_g*mu_g for every assignment.

Note lambda_c = 1 recovers the old M_g bound exactly, so the target is the smallest departure from uniform that works.

Do NOT try to read the rule off a solved instance: the dual is degenerate. At (1,1,2,4) the classes 38, 83 and 68 all have block profile (23,11,7,6,4,2) and receive 13/15, 7/15 and 0.
acceptance_criteria: An explicit lambda rule with a proof covering all assignments, or a written-up reason no simple rule exists.

title: verify_octave's expr errors don't say what expr is for
description:
A model that writes multi-statement Octave into verify_octave's expr gets Octave's raw 'eval: invalid use of statement list', or 'check_farkas undefined' when it tries to define a helper inline. Neither says what the harness actually wants: expr must be ONE expression reducing to a scalar logical, and anything that needs statements or helper functions goes through octave_eval first, which keeps them in the workspace.

Observed three times in five turns on gen-14 B2 (turns 33, 34, 35) while it was building a residual LP check. Each one costs a turn.

vf_check already refuses non-scalar and non-logical results with a message that explains itself ('wrap it in all(...) or any(...) to say which you mean').
